Dreadful
DRED-ful
adj.
From dread, Saxon draedan, to fear greatly, and the suffix -ful. Webster 1828: impressing dread; terrible; awful; venerable in the highest degree. The older English sense includes reverence, which is why Scripture can call God dreadful as praise.

Biblical Definition

Dreadful in the Authorized Version is not simply frightening; it carries the older sense of that which rightly commands awe, and Scripture uses it of God, of a place, of a day, and of a beast. Jacob wakes at Bethel and says the thing that the modern religious vocabulary has almost lost the power to say: And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven (Genesis 28:17). He is not complaining; he is worshipping. Daniel opens his great prayer of confession by naming God in the same register, and joining the terror to the covenant in one breath: O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments (Daniel 9:4). Malachi closes the Old Testament pointing forward: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). And Daniel uses the word for the fourth beast of the night vision: a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth (Daniel 7:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DREADFUL as impressing dread; terrible; frightful; formidable; and, in the older and higher sense, awful, venerable in the highest degree — that which is to be regarded with reverential fear.

expand to see more

DREADFUL, a. — Impressing dread; terrible; frightful; formidable to the mind.

Awful; venerable in the highest degree; to be regarded with reverential fear.

Inspiring awe by greatness, majesty, or holiness, as well as by danger.

Applied in Scripture to God, to His day, to holy places, and to the visions of judgment.

From dread, Saxon draedan, to fear greatly, and -ful, full of.

Key Scripture

Genesis 28:17 — "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."

Daniel 9:4 — "And I prayed unto the LORD my God, and made my confession, and said, O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments;"

Malachi 4:5 — "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD:"

Daniel 7:7 — "After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth: it devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it: and it was diverse from all the beasts that were before it; and it had ten horns."

Modern Corruption

Daniel 9:4 addresses God as great and dreadful in the same clause that names His covenant mercy, and the modern devotional register — which knows how to say tender and has no idea how to say dreadful — has quietly lost half of the biblical doctrine of God.

expand to see more

The two halves of Daniel’s address belong together and neither is safe alone. He prays to the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and the prayer that follows is one of the most thorough confessions in Scripture. A God who is only dreadful cannot be approached; a God who is only tender need not be confessed to. The contemporary evangelical vocabulary has almost entirely lost the first term. God is described as loving, welcoming, and near, and rarely as the One before whom Isaiah cried Woe is me! for I am undone, before whom John fell at His feet as dead, and of whom Hebrews 12:29 says our God is a consuming fire. The result is not warmer worship but thinner worship, since the tenderness means little if it is a temperament rather than a condescension.

Genesis 28:17 shows what recovery looks like. Jacob, a deceiver running from a brother he had cheated, wakes from a dream of angels and says How dreadful is this place! — and calls it the house of God and the gate of heaven in the same sentence. Awe and welcome are not alternatives to be balanced but a single response to a single God. Malachi 4:5 sets the same word over the last day, and it is the last verse but one in the Old Testament: the coming of the LORD is great and dreadful, and the promise attached is that hearts will be turned lest the earth be smitten with a curse.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yare (H3372), to fear, to reverence; nora (H3372 niphal participle), dreadful, to be feared; emah (H367), terror; Greek phoberos (G5398), fearful, terrible.

expand to see more

Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, to revere; its participle nora is the dreadful of Genesis 28:17 and Daniel 9:4.

Hebrew emah (H367) — terror, dread; a horror of great darkness fell upon him (Genesis 15:12).

Hebrew dechal (H1763) — Aramaic, to be afraid; dreadful and terrible of the fourth beast (Daniel 7:7).

Greek phoberos (G5398) — fearful, terrible; a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31).

Greek phobos (G5401) — fear; the root of the fear of the Lord in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 7:1).

Usage

"How dreadful is this place! (Genesis 28:17) — not a complaint but an act of worship."

"The great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy (Daniel 9:4) — terror and covenant mercy in one clause."

"The great and dreadful day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5) — the last word of the Old Testament but one."
